Curated neurodegeneration axis signals are sensitive to cell composition and analytic choices: an adversarial re-analysis of a transcriptomic scoring pipeline
papers.abstract: Background: Curated gene-set ("axis") scores are widely used to summarise disease biology in postmortem brain transcriptomes. In bulk tissue such scores can also change with cell-type composition, with broad transcriptome shifts in diseased tissue, or with analysis choices made after the results were seen. We tested these explanations on our own published pipeline, NeuroFate, whose preprint reported an Alzheimer's disease (AD) "neuronal vulnerability" axis and a Parkinson's disease (PD) "divergent" synuclein-mitochondrial axis. Results: A code audit found that the AD discovery axis averaged Sst, Pvalb and Lamp5 interneuron cell-type proportions together with its gene-expression features; that 90 endpoint x axis tests were run before the endpoints were locked; that axes were defined from the cohorts later cited as discovery evidence; and that the PD-divergent label came from an axis-specific rule defined after the result. Their contribution to the AD association could not be quantified because the donor-level data were not archived. In GSE7621 (16 PD, 9 controls) the synuclein-mitochondrial association reproduced (exact p = 0.0011) but depended on the scoring method (exact p from 0.001 to 0.057; with per-gene standardisation no axis reached Benjamini-Hochberg significance), lay at the 2.4th percentile of 10,000 expression-matched random probe sets (two-sided p = 0.06), and was attenuated by 76% (95% interval 26% to >100%) after adjustment for a dopaminergic-marker expression proxy (PD coefficient -1.13 to -0.27 SD). A small laser-captured cohort (GSE20141; 10 PD, 8 controls) was inconclusive: no axis reached p < 0.05, and the synuclein-mitochondrial effect had the same sign. In 1,000 simulated cohorts, a naive test called a purely composition-driven gene set significant in 82% of cohorts, whereas the proposed battery classified it as composition-independent in 5% while recovering a planted within-cell effect in 98% (moderate effect) and 50% (weak effect) of cohorts. Conclusions: The original axis associations do not establish composition-independent disease programs; their interpretation is sensitive to feature construction, scoring and adjustment for cell composition. Curated axis scores in bulk brain tissue should be reported with competitive null distributions, composition adjustment, exact small-sample inference, and endpoints and scoring fixed before analysis. We provide code for these checks.
affiliations: Maulana Azad College (corresponding author)

papers.title: Building computational benchmarks: an Omnibenchmark reimplementation of a single-cell preprocessing pipeline evaluation
papers.abstract: Background: In the past few years, we have seen a veritable surge in single-cell (e.g., RNA-sequencing) techniques and datasets, enabling increasingly detailed characterization of cellular heterogeneity across tissues and conditions. This surge in single-cell techniques has been complemented by a large number of analysis frameworks and pipelines, and a large parameter space and researcher degrees of freedom to use them. Many neutral benchmarks have been presented for various computational tasks, but most make design decisions that render them incompatible with each other, e.g., through the use of different datasets, metrics, or parameter sets. Results: We showcase Omnibenchmark, a recently developed framework to build reproducible, extensible, and standardized method comparisons for an arms-length benchmark that evaluates five single-cell RNA sequencing pipelines, spanning filtering, normalization, dimensionality reduction, and clustering, on three datasets. The framework facilitates the broad investigation of pipelines used in single-cell data analysis while highlighting how the process of building benchmarks can be streamlined and unified. This standardization enables benchmarks to be extended in several directions, including broader parameter sweeps, comparisons across software versions and architectures, isolation of pipeline steps, and integration of additional pipelines, datasets, and metrics. As an example, our harmonization of pipelines highlighted that tools implement the (clustering) resolution parameter differently. Conclusions: Omnibenchmark provides a reproducible, extensible, and standardized approach for benchmarking. By unifying the process of benchmark construction, it can facilitate more consistent method comparisons and provides a foundation for broader, more flexible, and more sustainable benchmarking efforts.
affiliations: University of Zurich (corresponding author)

papers.title: Optimisation of single-nuclei isolation and RNA sequencing of parasitic nematodes
papers.abstract: Single-cell/nuclei transcriptomics has revolutionised our understanding of cell, tissue, and organismal biology in humans and model organisms across health and disease. However, for non-model species, reassessment and refinement of conventional methods is needed to address novel technical and biological challenges. Here, we evaluate three established nuclei isolation protocols and, building on these experiences, develop an optimised protocol for single-nuclei isolation of parasitic nematodes (SNIP). SNIP recovered 1.7- to 4.1-fold more nuclei than the three established protocols, and 3.2-fold more RNA per nucleus than the best-performing of these. We validated SNIP across macroscopic and microscopic life stages and both sexes of two phylogenetically distinct gastrointestinal nematodes, Haemonchus contortus and Trichuris muris, and used it to generate single-nuclei RNA-seq data revealing sex- and stage-specific gene expression and putative tissue-specific expression in both species. By enabling flexibility with frozen samples and consistent recovery across diverse parasitic nematode life stages, SNIP provides a practical foundation for building cell and nuclei atlases in other non-model species, toward advancing understanding from fundamental biology to infection and disease.

papers.title: Genetic control and tissue specificity of transcriptomic rhythmicity
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms influence molecular traits in most tissues, yet genetic studies mostly treat molecular measurements as static. In particular, genetic effects on gene expression are typically investigated through expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) studies, which ignore sampling time and therefore miss genetic effects on rhythm parameters such as amplitude and acrophase. In this study, we used a cosinor-based joint genotype-by-rhythm interaction framework applied to GTEx version 10 gene expression data, with donor inferred phase as a proxy for circadian time. We first identified rhythmically expressed genes in 49 of the 50 tissues profiled in GTEx. We then tested common variants within 50 kb of each rhythmic gene's transcription start site for genetic regulation of transcriptomic rhythmicity. We identified 167 circadian expression QTLs (cd-eQTLs), comprising 54 lead signals for 51 genes across 28 tissues. Most cd-eQTLs altered oscillation amplitude, while others affected acrophase or both. We then investigated the tissue specificity of cd-eQTLs and found that those acting on core circadian genes had consistent effects across tissues, whereas those acting on clock-regulated genes were largely tissue-specific. A phenome-wide association study in the Pan-UK Biobank linked 34 cd-eQTLs to 100 phenotypes, including self-reported chronotype, adiposity, blood cell counts and blood biochemistry. These results show that genetic variation shapes circadian gene expression in a tissue-dependent manner, and that accounting for time of day reveals regulatory effects that static eQTL analyses cannot detect.

papers.title: scTGCL: A Transformer-Based Graph Contrastive Learning Approach for Efficiently Clustering Single-Cell RNA-seq Data
papers.abstract: Motivation: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables characterization of cellular heterogeneity at unprecedented resolution. However, accurate clustering of scRNA-seq data remains challenging due to high dimensionality, dropout-induced sparsity, and technical noise. Existing contrastive learning methods usually create augmented views by perturbing gene expression values, so the uncertainty in cell-cell relationships caused by dropout events is not properly modeled. Results: We propose scTGCL, a novel Transformer-based graph contrastive learning framework that learns robust and discriminative cell representations directly from gene expression data. scTGCL employs multi-head self-attention to adaptively construct weighted cell-cell graphs and a Transformer encoder to generate cell embeddings from them, capturing diverse biological relationships. For contrastive augmentation, we apply feature-level gene masking together with attention masking that randomly drops edges of the learned attention matrices, enabling the model to withstand dropout events and technical noise. A symmetric contrastive loss maximizes agreement between original and augmented representations, while joint optimization with reconstruction and imputation losses preserves biological interpretability. Extensive experiments on twenty real and simulated scRNA-seq datasets demonstrate that scTGCL achieves the highest average performance among nine state-of-the-art baseline methods in clustering accuracy, normalized mutual information, and adjusted Rand index, while also achieving superior imputation performance and substantially lower runtime on large-scale datasets. Furthermore, biological analysis confirms that the learned clusters align with known cell types and yield biologically interpretable pathway enrichment, validating the utility of scTGCL for downstream cell annotation and marker gene discovery. Availability and Implementation: The source code and test data are freely available at GitHub (https://github.com/ShoaibAbdullahKhan/scTGCL)

papers.title: Targeting SUFU-mediated GLI activity alleviates ciliopathic phenotypes
papers.abstract: Ciliopathies are incurable, pleiotropic diseases that result from defective cilia. Several ciliopathic phenotypes arise from improper processing and activity of GLI transcription factors, yet attempts to rescue these phenotypes by overexpressing activator or repressor GLI isoforms have proven unsuccessful. Here, we demonstrate that modulating SUFU-GLI interactions restores GLI transcriptional activity and rescues ciliopathic phenotypes in vivo. As previous work identified increased accumulation of SUFU in ciliopathic conditions, we hypothesized that exploiting SUFU's epistatic relationship to the cilium could provide a novel therapeutic strategy for ciliopathies. Genetic introduction of either a single null allele (Sufu+/-) or point mutation allele (SufuD159R), which modulates SUFU-GLI binding, into a ciliopathic mouse model revealed that both interventions improved midfacial phenotypes; however, SufuD159R provided a more complete rescue by significantly improving mandibular phenotypes as well. Molecular examination of this genetic modification revealed restored GLI3 binding to DNA, GLI3 interaction with transcriptional cofactors, and GLI3-directed transcription of target genes, collectively driving the rescue of numerous ciliopathic phenotypes. These findings reveal cilium-independent functions for SUFU and establish that modulating SUFU-GLI interactions bypasses the need for ciliary GLI processing. Together, these data provide a promising therapeutic approach for ameliorating ciliopathic pathologies.

papers.title: E2 displacement of CIP2A from TOPBP1 activates the DNA damage response during papillomavirus life cycles
papers.abstract: Prabhakar et al. show that HPV16 E2 rewires the DNA damage response during epithelial differentiation by displacing CIP2A from TOPBP1. This molecular switch inhibits PP2A, activates ATM, suppresses ATR signaling, and supports viral episome stability in HPV16-positive cells and lesions.

papers.title: BCLAF1 and responses to RAG-induced DNA breaks enforce pre-B cell checkpoint
papers.abstract: Schmidt et al. show pre-B cells in vivo transition through distinct subpopulations characterized by unique transcriptional programs. Progression through these subpopulations is maintained, in part, by signals from DNA breaks generated during immunoglobulin gene recombination, which contribute to preservation of the pre-B cell checkpoint.

papers.title: How the TREX-2 complex associates with the nuclear pore
papers.abstract: Obarska-Kosinska et al. combine cryo-electron tomography, AI-assisted modeling, and crosslinking mass spectrometry to build an extended model of the human nuclear pore. They identify five additional nucleoporins and show how the nuclear basket and TREX-2 complex are attached to the nuclear ring, revealing the spatial organization of mRNP export.

papers.title: Human CYP1A2 metabolism of organophosphorus pesticides and nerve agent surrogates
papers.abstract: CYP1A2 contributes 13-15% of hepatic CYP450 content and plays a critical role in the metabolism of approximately 10% of pharmaceutical drugs in the human body. CYP1A2 has been previously reported to bioactivate and detoxify both the thion (P=S) and oxon (P=O) forms of organophosphorus (OP) compounds. In this study, we determined the capacity of CYP1A2 to degrade OP compounds using LC-MS/MS, as well as the inhibition of its activity by OP compounds using the previously developed pFluor50 assay. CYP1A2 was selective in metabolizing thions over oxons, and several OP compounds inhibited its activity in a time- and dose-dependent manner. To further investigate the mechanism of CYP1A2-OP interactions, molecular docking studies were performed using a crystal structure of CYP1A2 (PDB ID: 2HI4). Linear correlation analysis between CYP1A2 inhibition at 10 M with 30 minute preincubation and the % OP compound remaining at 2 hours (R = -0.71, P<0.001) showed a moderate but significant correlation. Based on these findings, CYP1A2 was identified as a potential bioscavenger for OP compound metabolism, supporting the future integration of experimental and in silico data for developing artificial intelligence (AI) / machine learning (ML) models for prediction of CYP1A2-mediated metabolism of existing and emerging OP compounds, including those of toxicological and chemical warfare relevance.
affiliations: College of Pharmacy, Ohio State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Synovial fluid glycosaminoglycans signature involved 3-O-sulfated heparan sulfate modulated by TGF-β pathway in OA
papers.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) involved extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling of cartilage associated to inflammatory activation of fibroblastic like synoviocytes (FLS) from the synovium, but the molecular crosstalk between these two compartments remains poorly understood. Among Glycosaminoglycans (GAG) compound from ECM, heparan sulfate (HS) specifically regulate the bioavailability and activity of Heparin Binding Proteins (HBP), including cytokines and growth factors, such as TGF-{beta}, whose aberrant bioavailability in the synovial fluid (SF) could drive the catabolic process. Here, we investigated the composition, sulfation patterns and biological activities of GAG from OA SF that are currently uncharacterized and explored the regulation of 3-O-sulfated HS in TGF-{beta} mediated response in FLS. Total GAG from 52 OA-SF SF were extracted and quantitatively characterized by DMMB assay and HPLC. They are functional since they are able to bind several HBP with pleiotropic inflammatory and angiogenic properties according to ELISA competitive binding assay. They were able also to transactivate HBP signaling in cellular tests in-vitro, since they potentiated proliferative properties on fibroblastic and endothelial cells, and induced altered metabolic and inflammatory markers expressions in murine chondrocytes and human FLS. Although HS represented a minor fraction of SF-GAG, they contained a rare tri-sulfated disaccharidic fraction distinct from GAG from cartilage. Same GAG characterization was performed on FLS expanded from SF and SM samples. FLS exhibited also a rare sulfation pattern of 3-O-Sulfated HS on their surface analyzed by immunofluorescent staining, associated with the expression of 4 isoforms of 3-O-sulfotransferase (HS3ST) identified by RT-qPCR. TGF-{beta}1 treatment of FLS culture increases HS3ST expression profiles and HS sulfation pattern through the SMAD2/3 pathway, as observed by RT-qPCR, IF and western blot respectively. Finally, combined siRNA mediated silencing of these HS3ST enzymes affects FLS inflammatory secretome, according to proteome profiler cytokine arrays. among pro-inflammatory CXCL10 and CCL5 chemokines. Altogether, these data identify OA SF-GAG as new effective modulator of joint cell responses and reveal for the first time 3-O-sulfated HS and HS3ST patterns of expression in OA FLS associated with TGF-{beta}-Smad2/3-signaling pathway. Such specific HS fractions may contribute to the regulation of synovial inflammatory secretome, according to HBP partners that need to be further identified. However, this new glycanic mechanistic pathway sustaines the involvement of HS in OA progression and subsequently their interest as glycanic therapeutic targets.
affiliations: University Paris Est Creteil (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mathematical genomics of SRY proteins and their associated HMG-Box domains across mammals
papers.abstract: Male sex determination in mammals depends on sex-determining region Y (SRY), a transcription factor whose high-mobility group box (HMG box) binds and bends DNA to activate SOX9. The divergent N- and C-terminal domains lack sequence homology and have been dismissed as passive linkers, yet alignment-based homology cannot reveal whether they retain a hidden compositional grammar. We applied quantitative genomics to 65 full-length mammalian SRY proteins and 38 HMG-box subsequences across 75 mammals, integrating amino acid and dipeptide compositions, Shannon entropy, dominant-residue profiles, hydropathy-based n-gram spectra, longest hydropathy stretches, and cumulative proximity. The HMG box is tightly constrained: basic residues dominated, cysteine was nearly absent, entropy clustered near 4.0, polar content averaged 58.44\%, and 25 of 38 HMG boxes shared 57.97\% polar residues, whereas full-length SRY varied more, with rodents showing high polar and glutamine-rich profiles and cetaceans low polar content. Proximity-based clustering was more taxonomically consistent at the HMG level, while terminal regions blurred domain-level signals. Across 65 SRY proteins and 38 HMG domains, intrinsic disorder was the dominant predicted state, and a polyQ-rich rodent SRY illustrated how low-complexity repeats can produce misleading ordered predictions, underscoring the need for consensus disorder analysis in rapidly evolving intrinsically disordered regions. Cumulative proximity analysis identified \textit{Bos taurus} and \textit{Bos grunniens} as the only pair proximally clustered at both the full-length SRY and SRY-HMG levels, establishing multivariate proximity as a stringent criterion of compositional similarity satisfied by a single mammalian pair. These results suggest that SRY and its HMG box each carry a distinct compositional grammar, quantifiable only through alignment-independent signatures, with compositional individuality being the rule rather than the exception. These quantitative signatures provide a framework for interpreting SRY variation, assessing clinical mutations, and understanding evolutionary pressures shaping sex determination. Denser taxon sampling, structural modeling, and experimental tests are needed to clarify whether HMG-box drift and terminal-region variation affect DNA binding, bending, or reproductive function.

papers.title: In-Solution Measurements of Binding Kinetics and Thermodynamics by nano Temperature Alteration Kinetics
papers.abstract: Binding kinetics are central to mechanism-driven drug discovery. Previously, we established Spectral Shift technology for the measurement of equilibrium binding affinity by detecting small shifts in the emission spectrum of a fluorescently labeled molecule upon binding to a ligand. While slow binding kinetics can be observed as a gradual change toward equilibrium after mixing the binding partners, faster interactions often have already reached equilibrium once the measurement is started. Here, we extend Spectral Shift to the measurement of fast binding kinetics through a method termed "nano Temperature Alteration Kinetics" (nanoTAK). A rapid temperature step perturbs the binding equilibrium of an enthalpically driven interaction, and the subsequent relaxation toward the new equilibrium is monitored in real time by recording the time-dependent Spectral Shift signal. The relaxation directly encodes the association rate kon and dissociation rate koff of the interacting molecules, which are extracted by fitting data of a full ligand dilution series to a global kinetic model. In addition, the fit also returns thermodynamic parameters of the interaction such as the binding enthalpy and entropy. We validate the approach across three tiers of molecular interactions. First, hybridization of a 10-mer DNA duplex serves as a model system with large binding enthalpy. Global fits match the data over three different temperature steps and confirm the accuracy of the derived fit model. Second, the kinase p38 with a set of six ATP-competitive and allosteric inhibitors demonstrates that the method extends to a classical protein-small molecule system with substantially smaller enthalpic changes, yielding consistent rate constants across compounds and temperatures and offering unique insights into their temperature dependence. Third, the degrader system consisting of VHL E3-ligase complex (VCB), PROTAC MZ1 and bromodomain 2 of BRD4 (BRD4(BD2)) illustrates the application to a higher-order system, revealing differences in the binding kinetics between the binary and ternary complex. The presented method can resolve interactions that re-equilibrate faster than within ~1 second, a timescale that can be difficult to access reliably with surface-based instruments. Binding kinetics can be measured both near room temperature, using a temperature step from 20 to 25 {degrees}C, but also, as an inherent feature of the approach, at physiologically relevant temperatures such as 37 {degrees}C.

papers.title: Effects of panitumumab on the proteome of treated EGFRvIII glioblastoma cells and on their extracellular vesicles
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma (GB) is an aggressive brain tumor for which reliable biomarkers of therapeutic response are still needed. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) can carry molecular components derived from their parent cells, thereby providing information on changes associated with the tumor and treatments. Among potential biomarkers, epidermal growth factor receptor variant III (EGFRvIII), is found in more than 40% of GB patients and is associated with aggressive tumor behavior and therapeutic resistance. EGFRvIII has also been detected on the surface of EVs, suggesting its potential value for monitoring tumor-associated molecular changes. This study investigated the effects of panitumumab, an anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody, on the proteomic profiles of EVs derived from EGFRvIII cells. U87 and U87-EGFRvIII cells and their derived EVs were characterized before and after treatment. EGFRvIII expression in cells and EVs was assessed by Western blotting and flow cytometry. Proteomic analyses were performed on cell lysates and EVs before and after treatment. Our results demonstrate that panitumumab significantly reduced surface EGFRvIII on EVs derived from U87-EGFRvIII cells, whereas no significant decrease was observed in cell lysates. This suggests that treatment may affect EGFRvIII trafficking or its incorporation into EVs. The proteomic analysis highlighted much more changes in EVs than in their parental cells after treatment, particularly in proteins associated with extracellular matrix organization and collagen. Together, these results demonstrate that panitumumab treatment is associated with changes in protein profile from EVs derived from EGFRvIII cells suggesting that the panitumumab treatment might have an impact on cells that could be reflected on EVs released by glioblastoma cells. In conclusion, our results suggest that EVs derived from EGFRvIII cells could serve as a useful circulating biomarker for assessing treatment efficacy and for preventing treatment escape.
