papers.title: Computational identification of responding T cell clones from longitudinal repertoire sequencing
papers.abstract: T cells activate and expand upon interaction with cognate antigen, derived from pathogens or mutated proteins. T cell clones can be identified by their T cell receptor (TCR) which acts as a unique barcode to track their expansion. Longitudinal TCR sequencing can be used to track T cell responses to a large array of stimuli. However, experimental identification of T cell clones of interest is challenging, especially when information about the driving antigen is lacking. Computational identification based on clonal dynamics is an antigen-agnostic alternative. However, it is subject to sequencing noise and biological variability, and relies on the choice of particular timepoints that are compared to find expanding and contracting clones. We review existing methods for identification of responding T cell clones from TCR sequencing, and the strategies that have been used to account for noise. We highlight that most methods look for clones at specific timepoints, and discuss the need for unbiased methods to shed light on new dynamics. We showcase how to address these needs by proposing CloneSearch, a method to identify expanding and contracting T cell clones from longitudinal TCR sequencing which is agnostic to the time of stimulus and can account for the noise these clones are subject to. CloneSearch can recapitulate previously identified responses from published data, and expand the analysis to show identification of previously undetected responses from these same datasets.
affiliations: Ecole normale superieure (corresponding author)

papers.title: Reforestation without Belowground Recovery: Sediment Microbiomes and Organic Carbon in Caribbean Mangroves
papers.abstract: Mangrove reforestation is expanding across the Caribbean, but restoration success is still judged almost exclusively by tree survival and canopy cover. Whether the sediment microbiome, which governs carbon burial and nutrient cycling, follows the recovery of the vegetation remains largely unknown. We combined 16S rRNA gene metabarcoding (V4, Illumina MiSeq) with CHNS elemental analysis, pH and salinity measurements to compare sediment prokaryotic communities along 0-100 cm profiles in a reference, a reforested (Rhizophora mangle plantings since 2019) and an altered mangrove within the Las Dunas de Las Calderas Natural Monument, Dominican Republic (39 cores pooled into 28 depth-resolved composite samples). Reference sediments contained 2.5-5.5-fold more organic carbon (median 7.5% vs 3.0% in altered and 1.3% in reforested sediments), had higher C/N ratios and were less alkaline (pH 8.2 vs 8.8). Reference communities were more diverse and even, and differed in composition from both disturbed stands (pairwise PERMANOVA, R^2 ~ 0.09, adjusted P = 0.0015), whereas reforested and altered communities were statistically indistinguishable (R^2 = 0.04, P = 0.25). Disturbed sediments were dominated by Cyanobacteriota (~41-45% of reads), which tracked high pH, whereas reference sediments were enriched in Chloroflexota, Thermodesulfobacteriota and Thermoproteota, lineages linked to anaerobic degradation of complex organic matter and sulfate reduction. Depth structured communities by separating surface from subsurface layers, and sediment organic carbon and nitrogen were the only significant constraints in distance-based redundancy analysis. These results indicate that, within a few years of the first plantings (2019), reforestation had not restored the carbon-rich, anaerobic sediment habitat of the reference forest. We propose sediment organic carbon and microbial community structure as complementary indicators for mangrove restoration monitoring in the Caribbean.
affiliations: Instituto Especializado de Estudios Superiores Loyola (corresponding author)

papers.title: Dynamics of genotype frequencies in finite partially clonal populations under mutation and genetic drift
papers.abstract: Most eukaryotes reproduce using partial clonality. Yet we still lack population genetic models capable of efficiently reconstructing and predicting genotype frequency changes across generations, and of elucidating underlying evolutionary processes in longitudinally monitored partially clonal populations. Here, we develop a Wright-Fisher-like model describing the mean and variance of genotype frequencies through time at a single multi-allelic locus in finite partially clonal populations with mutation. We show that different initial conditions and clonality rates generate distinct genotype-frequency trajectories. Regardless of clonality rate, partially clonal populations converge toward the same equilibrium as fully sexual populations, determined solely by reciprocal mutation rates among alleles. Dynamics proceed in two phases: genotype frequencies first approach Hardy-Weinberg proportions, then evolve along the Hardy-Weinberg parabola until reaching equilibrium. Mean allele frequencies and gene diversity remain unaffected by clonality throughout these trajectories. Instead, clonality rate determines the speed at which populations return to Hardy-Weinberg proportions, thereby shaping the sequence of genotype-frequency distributions traversed over successive generations. The variance around mean trajectories depends on parental genotype frequencies and population size, and is not directly determined by clonality rate; rather, clonality affects it only indirectly by altering the sequence of genotype distributions traversed. This explains why partially clonal populations may exhibit both positive and negative FIS at different loci, and why variance in FIS among loci provides a robust proxy for inferring clonality rates. Our model provides a theoretical framework for analysing, predicting and interpreting temporal changes in genotype frequencies in monitored populations, establishing a foundation for future inference methods based on time-series genotyping data.
affiliations: INRAE (corresponding author)

papers.title: A hyperactivating mutation in formin-like 2 causes brain and vertebrae defects
papers.abstract: Formins are a group of proteins that nucleate and polymerize actin monomers into filaments to promote cell morphology and migration. Mutations in formin-encoding genes cause a broad spectrum of human diseases, ranging from kidney disease to non-syndromic intellectual disability. Through a forward genetics screen, we identified a mouse strain (nmf418) with a homozygous mutation in a splice acceptor in Fmnl2 that causes hindlimb motor dysfunction, enlarged midbrain colliculi, cerebellar hypoplasia, and vertebral abnormalities in the thoracolumbar spinal cord. The nmf418 mutation causes skipping of exon 10, which encodes a portion of the diaphanous inhibitory domain (DID) required for FMNL2 autoinhibition, and results in dramatically lower FMNL2 protein levels. Consistent with a gain-of-function mechanism, mutant FMNL2 has altered enrichment at filopodia tips, increased actin polymerization activity, and its expression results in enhanced cell migration in vitro. Furthermore, none of the neural or skeletal phenotypes were recapitulated in Fmnl2 knockout mice. Transcriptomic analysis of the embryonic cerebellum suggests that complete loss of Fmnl2 triggers broad compensatory upregulation of actin regulatory pathways, while expression of mutant FMNL2 is associated with dysregulation of cell migration, motility pathways, and calcium homeostasis pathways. Taken together, these findings suggest that Fmnl2 is largely dispensable for overall mouse development but that its autoregulation is essential for proper formation of the mouse nervous and skeletal systems.
affiliations: University of California San Diego (corresponding author)

papers.title: Position-dependent variant effects reveal importance of context in genomic regulation
papers.abstract: Massively Parallel Reporter Assays (MPRAs) provide a high-throughput framework for functionally characterizing how regulatory DNA sequences impact the expression of a model gene. MPRAs have also proven to be useful for measuring the effects of genetic variation, where each allele is typically tested in the center of ~200 bp of genomic context cloned into the MPRA; but the impact of variant position and local context remains largely unexplored. In this study, we systematically investigate how shifting the position of a variant within an MPRA probe influences its regulatory activity using models that predict expression in MPRAs from DNA sequence. We find that while the direction of variant effects is usually preserved across positions, the magnitude of expression changes can vary substantially depending on where the variant is placed within the construct. This positional bias appears to be largely explained by the strong position-dependent activity of TFs whose binding the variants perturb. In a subset of cases, interactions consistent with cooperativity between TFs also contribute to position-specific effects. ~1% of variants appear to disrupt RNA polymerase III (Pol III) promoters within Alu elements, resulting in position-specificity because both A and B boxes are required for function and exclusion of either motif due to window shifts disrupts the variants' effects. Consequently, this positional bias can lead to underestimating variant effect sizes from MPRAs, resulting in missed causal variants for downstream functional analyses. Our study demonstrates the complexity of cis-regulatory grammar and how regulatory assays used to study variants can confound their interpretation.
affiliations: The University of British Columbia (corresponding author)

papers.title: ssJSD: A fusion of sparsity and spatial information for HiC single-cell clustering
papers.abstract: Single-cell high-throughput chromatin conformation capture (scHiC) enables profiling three dimensional genome architecture at cellular resolution, providing insights into cell-to-cell variability and cellular functions. Recent frameworks utilize spatial interaction patterns to derive dissimilarity measures for downstream tasks such as cell clustering. However, the inherent sparsity and ultra-high dimensionality of scHiC contact matrices pose significant challenges. A central hurdle is that existing measures typically treat all zeros without distinction, failing to differentiate biologically meaningful structural zeros (SZs) from technical dropouts. Here, we introduce ssJSD (spatial and sparsity informed Jensen-Shannon Divergence), a computational framework designed to explicitly account for scHiC-specific sparsity patterns. By integrating band-wise contact frequency profiles with SZ-induced sparsity matrices, ssJSD leverages both spatial interaction patterns and biological absence of contacts. We adopted two complementary integration strategies: an early fusion approach that concatenates information into a single representation, and a late fusion approach that integrates JSD-based dissimilarities through diverse averaging methods. Through simulations and applications to human cell lines and prefrontal cortex data, we demonstrate that ssJSD improves clustering accuracy and effectively distinguishes cell types. Our study indicates that integrating SZ patterns is important for accurately quantifying cell-to-cell variability in 3D genomics.
affiliations: The Ohio State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A genomic foundation model for interpreting human genetic diversity
papers.abstract: Interpreting human genomes requires models that recognize shared biological functions while accounting for variation underlying traits, disease susceptibility and adaptation. Here we present hEVO, a genomic foundation model trained on 4.784 billion distinct haplotype sequences reconstructed from whole genome sequencing (WGS) data for 63,809 individuals selected from 550,237 samples across eight cohorts. Pretraining integrates shared sequence features and naturally occurring allelic differences without clinical or functional labels. Against representatives of the Evo 2, NT, GPN and other genomic model families, hEVO ranked first in 18 of 19 primary comparisons spanning functional annotation, variant interpretation and human evolution. Its pretrained allele scores generalized across all six complementary variant benchmarks without task-specific training, achieving the highest performance across clinical pathogenicity, fine-mapped causal variants and experimentally measured regulatory effects. Retrospective ClinVar reclassification further demonstrated improved identification of pathogenic classifications later downgraded, supporting reassessment of earlier clinical interpretations. Predictive strengths extended to ancestry inference, human accelerated sequences and preference for reported selected alleles. This breadth was achieved with substantially fewer parameters than billion-parameter comparators and low inference overhead in the evaluated workloads. These findings establish human haplotype diversity as a source of transferable biological information for interpreting both the disruption of genome function and the variation retained during human evolution.
affiliations: Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Center, Guangzhou Medical University, Guangzhou, China; Department of Bioinformatics, The Province and Ministry Co-sponso (corresponding author)

papers.title: Q-DOAS: A Proximity Quenching Assay for Real-Time Detection of Early Protein Aggregation Events
papers.abstract: Accurate measurement of protein aggregation is essential for studying neurodegenerative diseases. The standard ThT assay reports on amyloid formation but is blind to early oligomers and is prone to interference. We describe Q-DOAS, a plate-reader assay that quantifies protein self-assembly in real time via proximity-quenching of a single, site-specifically conjugated dye (BODIPY-TMR). Using mutant Huntingtin-exon 1 (mHTT-Ex1) and -Synuclein A53T, we show Q-DOAS detects pre-amyloid oligomers, yielding quantitative kinetic data compatible with mechanistic analysis. We demonstrate its utility to dissect mutational effects, screen for protein and small-molecule inhibitors, and quantify amyloid seeding activity in cellular and mouse models of Huntington's disease. Q-DOAS also detects seeds in cerebrospinal fluid from Parkinson's disease patients without amplification. Q-DOAS provides a sensitive, robust, and scalable tool for studying the earliest events in amyloid pathologies and for advancing therapeutic development.
affiliations: Stanford University (corresponding author)

papers.title: High-throughput glioblastoma-neurovascular assembloids model blood-tumor barrier disruption, tumor reprogramming and therapeutic efficacy
papers.abstract: The blood-tumor barrier (BTB) in glioblastoma is an abnormal neurovascular interface that can be focally leaky yet still restrict effective therapy. We present a rapid human BTB model in which patient derived glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs), human brain endothelial cells, pericytes and astrocytes selfassemble within 72 hours into uniform three-dimensional "BTB assembloids". Thousands can be generated in parallel in standard plates, enabling high-throughput studies and drug testing. These assembloids establish spatial glioma-vascular and glioma-astrocyte niches with focal loss of endothelial tight-junction proteins, astrocyte recruitment and endothelial recruitment toward tumor clusters with localized junctional disruption at the tumor-vascular interface. BTB-conditioned GSCs acquire more invasive, stemness, mesenchymal and angiogenic programs compared with matched GSC neurospheres, and these BTB-conditioned states translate into greater engraftment and infiltrative growth in vivo, accompanied by vascular remodeling and BTB-like barrier disruption. The assembloid platform supports quantitative, "barrier-aware" assessment of compound access and retention in human BTB- (and BBB)-like contexts, revealing that functional P-glycoprotein efflux persists despite increased BTB permeability, thereby dissociating structural barrier leakiness from therapeutic accessibility. It is modular and compatible with iPSC-derived brain cells (for example brain endothelial cells), microglia or other immune components, thereby providing a route toward genotypeand immunity-specific modeling. Together, this establishes BTB assembloids as a scalable human system to interrogate glioblastoma-neurovascular crosstalk and to evaluate brain-tumor therapeutics.
affiliations: Brigham and Women's Hospital (corresponding author)

papers.title: The RdRp Thumb-1 Pocket is a Conserved Target for Broad-Spectrum Antiviral Development
papers.abstract: RNA viruses cause human diseases ranging from mild colds to deadly pandemics. Direct-acting, broad-spectrum, non-nucleoside antivirals have been characterized as impossible to develop because allosteric binding sites are poorly conserved. The HCV NS5B RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) Thumb-1 allosteric site and its interaction with the HCV NS5B {Lambda}1-loop governs an essential conformational change required for polymerase initiation. The only approved NS5B Thumb-1 inhibitor, beclabuvir, has been shown to be inactive against a broad panel of non-HCV viruses, including poliovirus, rhinovirus, coronavirus, coxsackievirus, influenzavirus, and HIV. A conserved, homologous allosteric site on RdRp that spans multiple viral families has not been reported. Here, we report GALILEO's discovery that the Thumb-1 pocket, its associated {Lambda}1-loop and their interaction are conserved across RNA viral families for the first time. The discovery is structurally validated through comparative analysis of Protein Data Bank (PDB) deposited viral polymerases utilizing a method that allows independent, public validation. We further demonstrate that beclabuvir's dependence on its indole C6 carbonyl to interact with the HCV-specific residue R503 restricts its activity to HCV. The discovery is biochemically validated with MDL-001, which does not contain a C6 carbonyl substituent. MDL-001 directly blocks viral RNA synthesis in isolated HCV and SARS-CoV-2 replication complexes and selects for the canonical Thumb-1 resistance mutation P495S in HCV NS5B. The discovery is validated at the cellular level through demonstration of MDL-001's broad-spectrum, in vitro inhibition of both HCV and SARS-CoV-2. Preclinical proof of concept and development of MDL-001 across HCV, HBV, HDV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and RSV have been previously reported. These findings establish RdRp Thumb-1 as a conserved allosteric pocket and a druggable target for broad-spectrum direct-acting antiviral development.
affiliations: Model Medicines (corresponding author)

papers.title: Metagenomic contextualization of proteins with state space models
papers.abstract: Genomic foundation models have emerged as powerful tools for learning representations of biological sequences, but existing approaches predominantly rely on Transformer architectures, whose quadratic attention complexity limits their ability to capture long-range genomic context. This limitation is particularly relevant for metagenomics, where sequencing data have increased more than 500-fold since 2011, generating increasingly large and diverse datasets. For example, gLM2, a Transformer-based mixed-modality genomic language model, was trained with a context window of 4,096 tokens, limiting its ability to capture extended genomic context within metagenomic contigs. Developing scalable architectures capable of processing longer sequences while integrating protein and nucleotide information is therefore essential for advancing genomic foundation models. We introduce Nammu, a 167-million-parameter, bidirectional Mamba-based genomic foundation model that integrates protein and nucleotide sequences within a 20,000-token context window. Leveraging the linear scaling of state-space models, Nammu was trained using a curriculum learning strategy on the OpenMetaGenomic (OMG) corpus, first incorporating 64 million protein sequences followed by 32 million mixed-modality metagenomic contigs. Despite using approximately 37\% fewer training tokens than gLM2, Nammu outperformed this Transformer-based model in taxonomic classification across all evaluated taxonomic ranks on a marine metagenomic dataset from the Critical Assessment of Metagenome Interpretation (CAMI). On the exact-feature-unmatched CAMI II Strain Madness test set, Nammu achieved higher all-contig genus-classification accuracy than Kraken2 (0.9182 versus 0.8142). Nammu further outperformed gLM2 (150M) in KEGG Orthology prediction using deep-sea metagenome-assembled genomes. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of state-space architectures for scalable, multimodal genomic representation learning and highlight their ability to support accurate taxonomic and functional predictions from metagenomic sequences.
affiliations: Oregon State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: HiChIA-Rep quantifies the similarity between enrichment-based chromatin interactions datasets
papers.abstract: Background: Enrichment-based 3D genome mapping technologies ChIA-PET, HiCAR, and related methods each yields a two-dimensional (2D) pairwise contact matrix encoding chromatin interaction frequencies and a one-dimensional (1D) coverage vector, indicating protein binding or chromatin accessibility. However, a lack of accessible and interpretable computational tools to quantify the similarity between these datasets prevents rigorous data quality assessment and biological implications. Results: We developed HiChIA-Rep, an efficient algorithm incorporating both 1D and 2D signals to measure similarity via graph signal processing methods. Implemented in Python, HiChIA-Rep takes standard file format as inputs: .hic, .bedpe for 2D contact matrix and .bigwig or .bedgraph for 1D coverage vector. HiChIA-Rep utilizes 1D and 2D signals effectively to distinguish biological replicates from non-replicates, cell lines, experiment types, and protein factors, often outperforming existing tools. In addition, HiChIA-Rep can evaluate specific genomic regions of interest, and its utility is demonstrated for correlating differential gene expression and transcriptional chromatin interactions mediated by RNA Polymerase II in MCF10A and MCF7 cell lines. Conclusions: HiChIA-Rep is readily applicable to existing ChIA-PET, HiChIP, PLAC-seq, HiCAR, and ChIATAC data. More broadly, HiChIA-Rep provides a graph signal processing framework to jointly analyze 1D and 2D signals, paving the ways to incorporate and interpret multiple data modalities probed by the emerging single-cell multi-ome methods in the future. We expect HiChIA-Rep to be a fundamental tool for the 3D genomics community.
affiliations: Gilbert S. Omenn Department of Computational Medicine and Bioinformatics, University of Michigan (corresponding author)

papers.title: CompleteBin: A transformer-based framework unlocks microbial dark matter through improved short contig binning
papers.abstract: Metagenomic binning is crucial for reconstructing microbial genomes from metagenomes. However, existing tools perform poorly in complex communities, where short contigs from low-abundance organisms predominate. This limits the deciphering of community composition and the functions it encodes. Here we present CompleteBin, a Transformer-based framework that bins contigs as short as 850 bp by combining context-based sequence tokenization, taxonomic embeddings from a Transformer pre-trained on reference genomes, and dynamic multi-view contrastive learning. We benchmarked CompleteBin against five binners using 80 CAMI II and 54 real-world metagenomes, yielding 111 CAMI II evaluation instances through the use of both gold-standard and independently assemblies. AMBER evaluation showed that CompleteBin achieved the highest base-pair-level F1 score in every CAMI II dataset across single-sample, multi-sample and co-assembly modes. CompleteBin also generally recovered more near-complete (NC) and medium-quality-or-higher (MQ+) metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) in both CAMI II and the real-world datasets. In cold-seep sediments, CompleteBin recovered 227 MQ+ strain-level genome bins (StGBs) that no other binner did, spanning 33 phyla. Contigs assigned to MQ+ MAGs only by CompleteBin encoded 473,671 non-redundant genes. Community-scale metabolic modelling further identified 777 StGBs encoding both complete nitrate and sulfate reduction pathways, 154 of which were not fully recovered by other binners, highlighting understudied microbial contributors to local element cycling.
affiliations: Hong Kong Baptist University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Aurora kinase A enables collective invasion and metastasis by endowing a leader cell phenotype and stabilizing cohesion with follower cells
papers.abstract: The metastatic process initiates with collective cell invasion into surrounding tissues and axillary nodes, and subsequent colonization at a distant site. Previously, we found collective invasion is augmented during the G2 cell cycle phase, facilitated through Aurora kinase A (AURKA)-mediated centrosome polarization in the leader cell. Here, we identify cell cycle-associated gene signatures as overrepresented in axilla and liver metastatic sites, with AURKA expression strongly correlated with breast cancer metastasis signatures, and pan-cancer patient survival. Then, we show GFP-AURKA expression endows breast epithelia cells with the ability to form outgrowths within immune-incompetent chicken embryos. Multi-parametric imaging of wound closure assays reveals phenotypes enabled by, and dependent upon AURKA expression. We discover leader cells express AURKA and acquire front-polarized centrosomes, which differentiates them from other cells in the migrating group. Ectopic expression of GFP-AURKA induces a leader cell phenotype. Conversely, inhibition of AURKA activity alters actin dynamics, promotes turnover of cell contacts, and reduces coordination within migrating groups. Specifically, AURKA interacts with the actin regulator EPLIN, and AURKA inhibition localizes EPLIN to lamellipodia and away from E-cadherin-positive contacts. Inhibiting these necessary roles for AURKA may provide a critical barrier against the metastatic spread of human breast carcinoma cells.
affiliations: Department of Pediatrics, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada V5Z 4H4 (corresponding author)

papers.title: Rewiring central carbon metabolism reveals a trade-off between yield and production rate in poly-γ-glutamic acid synthesis by Bacillus subtilis
papers.abstract: Improving carbon yield and process time is a key requirement for the industrially viable production of biopolymers. During poly-{gamma}-glutamic acid production with Bacillus subtilis, a considerable fraction of the carbon source is diverted into by-products. These originate from accumulating pyruvate, constraining carbon flux towards glutamate synthesis. Disrupting by-product pathways reduces their secretion, but the underlying imbalance at the pyruvate node persists. Here, we rewired the central carbon metabolism to redirect glycolytic flux from pyruvate formation towards oxaloacetate and 2-oxoglutarate in an improved medium. Deletion of pyruvate kinase combined with heterologous expression of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase established an alternative anaplerotic entry route into the TCA cycle. Subsequent disruption of gluconeogenetic reactions (OF5) reduced by-product formation by 81% and increased {gamma}-PGA yield to 0.41 g g-1 glucose, but lowered the glucose uptake rate. Alternatively, disruption of the TCA cycle downstream of 2-oxoglutarate combined with enhanced glutamate synthesis (OF4.2) increased substrate uptake and improved the {gamma}-PGA production rate by 39% compared to the wild type, while product and by-product titers remained comparable. Both strategies thus revealed a trade-off between improved yield or production rate. Subsequent 13C metabolic flux analysis and intracellular metabolite profiling revealed distinct carbon routing phenotypes. While strain OF5 maintained carbon within the TCA cycle, OF4.2 cycled carbon between oxaloacetate, malate and pyruvate, thereby altering redox and energy balances. These results highlight the need for coordinated control of carbon flux, redox metabolism and energy supply for improving {gamma}-PGA synthesis, and identify the oxaloacetate-malate-pyruvate node as a promising strain engineering target.
affiliations: RWTH Aachen University (corresponding author)

papers.title: MiR-208b-3p is an upstream regulator of redox-associated cardiomyocyte survival
papers.abstract: Background: Cardiac stress induces MYH6-to-MYH7 remodeling and activates redox-defense programs, but the regulatory mechanisms that distinguish adaptive from maladaptive stress responses remain incompletely defined. We investigated the role of miR-208b-3p, an intronic MYH7 microRNA, in cardiac stress adaptation. Methods and Results: We integrated myocardial transcriptomic and small RNA sequencing from stress-adapted Mlp-/- mice and human cardiomyopathy to identify stress-adaptive programs associated with preserved myocardial viability and complemented these analyses with in vivo miR-208b-3p inhibition and cellular gain-of-function experiments. Mlp-/- hearts exhibited marked Myh7 induction accompanied by an {approx}20-fold increase in miR-208b-3p, whereas this coordinated response was blunted in human end-stage dilated and ischemic cardiomyopathies. In vivo inhibition of miR-208b-3p selectively reduced Myh7, without altering Myh6 or baseline cardiac function. This reduction in Myh7 occurred without induction of established Myh7 transcriptional repressors, and miR-208b-3p gain-of-function similarly reduced MYH7 while suppressing several canonical repressors, indicating that its relationship with MYH7 extends beyond the established repressor pathway. miR-208b-3p inhibition activated oxidative stress, NRF2, autophagy, and cell-survival pathways. Oxidative stress transiently suppressed miR-208b-3p, with rebound induction after stress removal, whereas antioxidant treatment increased its expression. Pharmacological NRF2 activation did not alter miR-208b-3p, whereas miR-208b-3p gain-of-function reduced oxidative stress-associated apoptotic signaling and suppressed ATM, a predicted target and regulator of cellular stress responses, supporting an upstream role for miR-208b-3p in stress adaptation. Conclusions: MiR-208b-3p is a dynamic component of cardiac stress adaptation that links myosin remodeling with redox and survival responses. Its regulation of ATM and association with NRF2-related stress responses support an upstream role in coordinating cellular adaptation to cardiac stress.
affiliations: Karolinska Institutet (corresponding author)

papers.title: Delocalized DNA holes imprint mutation position in mismatch-repair-deficient cancers
papers.abstract: One electron oxidation of DNA generates migrating holes that come to rest at guanine runs, a positional pattern of damage characterized in vitro but not shown to reach somatic mutation in human cancer. In mismatch repair deficient gastric, colorectal and endometrial tumours, we find G>T substitutions within guanine runs enriched at the 5' guanine (0.86~0.87) and depleted at the 3' guanine (0.05~0.08), specific to G>T and near identical across all three cancer types. The profile along runs of two to five guanines, including the flattening of the profile as runs lengthen, matches the charge density computed for a delocalized hole without fitting (r = 0.87~0.93); treating the transfer integral as the only free parameter returns 0.073~0.088 eV from four datasets: three tumour cohorts, and mismatch-repair-knockout cells grown without added damage that share no part of the tumour pipeline. A defined one electron oxidant reproduces the asymmetry in repair proficient cells, and the asymmetry is undiminished among clonal mutations, where oxidation introduced during library preparation cannot reach. Guanine ionization energy nonetheless does not predict the genomic distribution of C>A substitutions, in any oxidative stratum of non hypermutated tumours or in the reference signature attributed to reactive oxygen species, delimiting where this chemistry reaches the cancer mutation spectrum.
affiliations: Seoul National University Bundang Hospital (corresponding author)

papers.title: China picks first researchers for 15-year mega grants

Nature’s job-satisfaction survey highlights the changing geography of science

Vast new fossil record challenges story of Earth’s ‘big five’ mass extinctions
Can a human survive in a whale’s belly? The science behind the thriller Whalefall
Body-clock disruptions contribute to one in four cases of depression, suggests large study

Universal platform for rapid green surface functionalization of diverse porous membranes for sustainable water treatment

Regulatable in vivo gene expression via adaptamers
papers.abstract: Bryant et al. develop adaptamers, compact RNA switches that use FDA-approved drugs to control gene expression by co-opting endogenous RNA-editing machinery rather than relying on foreign proteins. In mice, this approach safely tuned a metabolic hormone to reverse obesity, pointing to a simpler path toward programmable, drug-controlled gene therapies.

papers.title: Proteome-wide C-degron activity profiling connects conditional regulation of the CTLH E3 ligase complex to ribosome biogenesis
papers.abstract: Exploiting ORFeome libraries with different C-terminal architectures, Grant et al. perform comparative stability profiling to identify a conditionally regulated C-degron pathway governed by the CTLHMuskelin E3 ligase complex. Its substrate AAMP is the human ortholog of yeast Sqt1 and acts similarly as a uL16 chaperone, connecting nutrient status to control of ribosome biogenesis.

papers.title: Polycystin-2 functions as a calcium leak channel under endoplasmic reticulum stress to protect against myocardial ischemia
papers.abstract: Metabolically hungry organs such as the heart require a continual supply of energy from the mitochondria when stressed. Vuchkovska et al. show that the calcium channel polycystin-2 provides direct calcium transfer from the endoplasmic reticulum to the mitochondria to ensure this energy demand is met.

papers.title: METTL4 interacts with histone methylation readers MRG1/2 to regulate alternative splicing and promote thermomorphogenesis in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Warm temperature conditions affect morphology and architecture of plants. Zhu et al. showed that N6-2′-O-dimethyladenosine methyltransferase METTL4 interacts with histone methylation reader MRG1/2 to regulate alternative splicing of brassinosteroid signaling genes and promotes thermomorphogenesis in Arabidopsis.

papers.title: The TCF-1-E-protein axis preserves stem-like Th17 identity and prevents autoimmune pathology
papers.abstract: Han et al. show that TCF-1 deficiency in Th17 cells exacerbates autoimmune neuroinflammation. They uncover a reciprocal TCF-1-E-protein transcriptional circuit that preserves stem-like Th17 identity and prevents pathogenic conversion. Disruption of this circuit unleashes pathogenic Th17 cells, revealing a critical checkpoint in autoimmune disease.

papers.title: SMURFs regulate mesendoderm differentiation through SMAD2-dependent ubiquitination of CDK9
papers.abstract: Shin et al. show that the E3 ligases SMURF1/2 promote embryonic stem cell differentiation by controlling CDK9 stability. SMURF-mediated ubiquitination limits CDK9-dependent RNA polymerase II pause release at SMAD2 target genes, enabling progression beyond mesendoderm. Loss of SMURF1/2 stabilizes CDK9 and sustains SMAD2-dependent transcription of mesendodermal genes.

papers.title: An engineered probiotic for diagnosis and mucosal healing in inflammatory bowel disease
papers.abstract: Zhao et al. engineer an ROS-responsive probiotic that detects intestinal inflammation and delivers IL-22-Fc in situ. In mouse and piglet colitis models, this probiotic activates IL-22R1/STAT3 signaling, driving epithelial regeneration and restoring intestinal barrier integrity, establishing an integrated platform for IBD diagnosis and mucosal repair.

papers.title: A MADS51 allele is associated with flowering-time divergence and contributes to ecological adaptation during wild rice speciation
papers.abstract: Flowering-time divergence contributes to ecological adaptation and speciation. Zhang et al. identify MADS51 as a contributor to flowering-time divergence between Oryza rufipogon and O. nivara. A derived MADS51 haplotype in O. nivara promotes earlier flowering and shows signatures of positive selection, providing insights into flowering-time evolution.

papers.title: Multi-omics profiling of the choroid plexus reveals developmental cellular remodeling, early immune gene activation, and epithelial cell heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Fernandes, Andersson-Li, et al. present a transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility atlas of the lateral ventricle choroid plexus cells across postnatal and young adult stages in rodents, providing a resource for studying choroid plexus maturation and function.

papers.title: Asymmetric crosstalk between the BMP and TGF-β pathways resolves signaling ambiguity
papers.abstract: Auth et al. show that cells resolve ambiguity between opposing BMP and TGF-β cues through asymmetric crosstalk that favors TGF-β-driven responses. Mathematical modeling and experiments reveal that promiscuous SMAD heterocomplex formation redirects BMP-associated mediators toward TGF-β transcriptional targets, providing a computational mechanism for integrating conflicting signals and controlling cell fate.

papers.title: Small-molecule modulation of VDAC enhances glucose-stimulated insulin secretion by promoting ATP flux
papers.abstract: Enhancing insulin secretion is a major therapeutic strategy for diabetes. Matsunaga et al. identify DPEU, a small molecule that promotes mitochondrial ATP export through VDACs to enhance glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. Their findings establish VDAC-mediated ATP flux as a therapeutic mechanism for potentiating insulin secretion.

papers.title: Gut-derived glucagon-like peptides attenuate T cell-induced intestinal injury
papers.abstract: Koehler et al. demonstrate distinct physiological roles for GLP-1R and GLP-2R signaling in protecting the intestine from αCD3-induced enteropathy. Conversely, GLP-1R/GLP-2R agonists, administered separately or together, attenuate the heightened intestinal damage induced by T cell activation in mice with selective loss of intestinal proglucagon gene expression.

papers.title: The next click in antibody drug conjugate development
CD47 fuels intestinal fibrosis by inducing fibroblast phagocytic evasion and represents a therapeutic target
papers.abstract: CD47 marks a pathogenic fibroblast state in intestinal fibrosis, creating a phagocytic-evasion niche with macrophages via IL-1β crosstalk. Blocking this checkpoint restores macrophage clearance of fibroblasts and attenuates fibrosis, establishing CD47-SIRPα as a therapeutic target for Crohn’s disease complications.

papers.title: 20 years of iPSCs: From cellular reprogramming to clinical translation
From genome editing to chromosome engineering in plants
papers.abstract: Engineering large genomic segments is rapidly expanding the scope of plant genome manipulation from individual genes to chromosome-scale redesign. Recent advances in double-strand break-, prime-editing-, recombinase-, and transposase-based technologies now enable programmable deletion, insertion, replacement, duplication, inversion, and translocation of DNA fragments ranging from kilobases to megabases. In this review, we summarize the major strategies for large-fragment genome engineering in plants, compare their strengths and limitations, and discuss their applications in both fundamental plant biology and crop breeding. We further highlight that the integration of artificial intelligence is catalyzing the rapid optimization of large-fragment genome engineering. The ongoing transition from genome editing to chromosome engineering promises to revolutionize crop breeding and plant synthetic biology, ultimately enabling rational design of plant genomes.

papers.title: Modular in vivo engineering of the reductive methylaspartate cycles for synthetic CO2 fixation
papers.abstract: Rainaldi et al. design and computationally analyze four synthetic carbon-fixation cycles, two of which have higher theoretical biomass yield than existing alternatives. Using growth-coupled selection in Escherichia coli, they validate different modules, achieve CO2-dependent growth via the fastest known carboxylase, and establish a fourth pathway for acetate assimilation.

papers.title: Data storage with amino acid sequences
papers.abstract: Amino acid sequences in peptides and proteins can be used to store data with the advantages of high capacity and stability, offering a solution for storing ever-increasing amounts of data. Compared with peptides, proteins have longer sequences and can be produced at a much lower cost, enabling more efficient data storage and allowing specific functions to be incorporated using established protein techniques. Although data storage using peptides and proteins has been demonstrated, challenges related to cost, throughput, error rates, data density, and scalability remain to be addressed. Emerging technologies to overcome these challenges are under active development, and their successful commercialization could drive a paradigm shift, enabling high-density and very long-term data storage.

papers.title: Timed binary WNT activity is sufficient to model the early human neural axis
papers.abstract: The vertebrate nervous system develops into functionally distinct domains along the body axis[1]. Developmental studies implicate multiple signaling pathways in coordinating this process, but the order of specification events, sufficiency of individual signals, and molecular basis of competency remain unclear [2,3], leaving the field without a unified model of neuraxis patterning. Enteric nervous system (ENS) and midbrain dopaminergic (mDA) progenitors have reached clinical and preclinical testing [4-11], yet neither is produced at full purity, and yields vary markedly across human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC) lines, reflecting incomplete control of axial identity. Here we use single-cell genetic fate mapping to demonstrate that hPSCs can commit to anterior or posterior cranial fate within the first 24 hours of differentiation, before neural induction. Building on this finding, we show that the duration of a single saturating WNT pulse is sufficient to specify three 'first-order' domains: anterior cranial (0 h), posterior cranial (24 h) and trunk (48 h), each pre-neural and competent for CNS, neural crest and epidermal lineages. Nested 'second-order' domains are specified within first-order domains in response to WNT, FGF, and retinoic acid. Mechanistically, an anterior gene regulatory network repressing WNT targets is irreversibly shut down during the transition to posterior identities. Applying this binary WNT patterning logic, we generate mDA neurons and ENS progenitors robustly across hPSC lines and establish an assembloid model combining first-order progenitors to produce all major regions of the nervous system.
affiliations: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Spatial multi-omics implicates vascular adipocytes proximal to tertiary lymphoid structures in human aortic aneurysm and B-cell autoreactivity.
papers.abstract: Objective: Perivascular Adipose Tissue (PVAT), tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS), and the B lymphocytes they harbor have been implicated in regulating vascular diseases, including abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). Yet, the relationship of adipose tissue to TLS and B-cell responses is poorly understood. Approach and Results: Here, using multi-omics approaches, we characterized the potential interplay of vascular adipocytes and TLSs in shaping microenvironments conducive to pathogenic B-cell immunity in human AAA pathology. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing identified white adipocytes expressing transcripts for lipogenesis, lipolysis, and extracellular remodeling. Unexpectedly, these adipocytes expressed haptotactic and chemotactic factors such as thrombospondin 1 and autotaxin, and extracellular matrix proteins with potential to recruit CD44+ leukocytes within AAAs. Immunohistology revealed two anatomical compartments for the adipocytes within AAAs: PVAT and the medial-adventitial region. Medial-adventitial adipocytes were frequently associated with CD44+ TLSs and were largely absent from control non-aneurysmal abdominal aortas. Visium HD spatial transcriptomics revealed mature TLSs recapitulated the organization of functional secondary lymphoid structures, with multiple B-cell follicles clustered to form a nodular structure partly covered by a layer of smooth muscle cells. The TLSs harbored isotype-switched B cells expressing IgG1, IgG3, or IgA, with dominant kappa chain usage and IgG antibodies to the aortic wall. Myeloid cells in AAA were implicated in promoting B-cell effects, as they were the primary producers of B-cell activating factor (BAFF), a cytokine that promotes B-cell infiltration, survival, and function. Conclusion: Altogether, our results support a model in which new adipocytes in the medial-adventitial layer elicit inflammatory pathways that promote early TLS formation, and BAFF produced by myeloid cells promotes the survival and maturation of vascular wall-antigen-exposed B cells, leading to mature TLS formation, production of antibodies to AAA antigens, fueling inflammation and AAA growth.
affiliations: Brody School of Medicine, East Carolina University (corresponding author)

papers.title: CCTP-Atlas: Compartment-Resolved Ciliary Transcriptional Dysregulation in Tetralogy of Fallot, A Six-Dataset Integrative Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: Background. Primary cilia coordinate Hedgehog-dependent outflow tract morphogenesis. Concurrent human genetics implicates ciliary loss-of-function in nonsyndromic tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) risk, yet compartment-resolved ciliary transcriptional programmes in public TOF snRNA-seq remain unmapped at module resolution. Methods. We curated a Cardiac Ciliary Transcriptomic Panel (CCTP; 1,611 genes; four modules) and executed a ten-phase integrative pipeline on six public sc/snRNA-seq resources. Differentially expressed gene tables were harmonised (adjusted p < 0.05; |log2FC| [≥] 0.5 where available), mapped to CCTP modules, and tiered by evidence strength. Patient-level pseudobulk (three TOF versus five donors), permutation-validated Compartment Dysregulation Index (CMDI), Cross-Species Concordance Score (CSCS), STRING protein-protein interaction analysis, and diffusion pseudotime on 17,290 Ho organoid cells were performed. Results. Among 1,263 unique CCTP-associated hits, 396 genes recurred in at least two dataset tables (exploratory tier; Tier A endothelial anchor n = 24 from Zulibiya et al.). Only Zulibiya endothelial M1 structural-assembly CMDI exceeded a module-size-matched permutation null (p = 0.015). Patient-level pseudobulk returned zero false-discovery-rate-significant CCTP genes. CCTP-conditioned overlap with recent ciliary genetics was non-significant (Fisher p {approx} 0.13). Ho organoid pseudotime showed highest M1/M2 activity at day 8, declining toward day 21. Genome-wide CSCS classified 11 genes as fully conserved and 136 as partially conserved among scoreable orthologs. Conclusions. Ciliary transcriptional correlates in TOF are compartment-specific and module-structured, with the strongest inferential signal in TOF endothelium (M1). CCTP-Atlas provides a reproducible, tiered prioritisation resource linking public TOF snRNA-seq, organoid maturation proxies, and partial cross-species patterns. Findings are hypothesis-generating and complement but do not replicate recent ciliary genetics evidence until expanded cohorts and functional validation are performed. Data availability. Processed gene lists, manifests, and scripts. Source datasets: GSE203274, GSE168464, GSE166462, GSE126128; Li et al. (2025) supplementary tables. This is a preprint and has not been peer-reviewed.
affiliations: Riphah International University, Faisalabad (corresponding author)

papers.title: How AlphaFold 3 helps with multiscale drug discovery
papers.abstract: AlphaFold 3 (AF3) predicts protein ligand complexes, but the utility of its confidence scores for drug discovery remains unclear. We benchmarked AF3 interaction scores against BANDOCK+, an experimentally informed approach, using approved drugs and human protein libraries. AF3 ipTM achieved slightly higher observed aggregate disease ranking scores in a matched 1,103 protein comparison, with performance varying among individual indications. BANDOCK+ enabled substantially broader protein coverage using a computationally less demanding approach, including a 20,158 protein reference library. These findings highlight the potential of AF3 confidence scores for computational drug discovery and the tradeoffs between predictive performance and scalability.
affiliations: University at Buffalo (corresponding author)

papers.title: DCAF: Unifying Data Validity, Evaluation Validity and Predictive Modeling for Single-cell Perturbation Simulation
papers.abstract: Single-cell perturbation profiling is limited by cost and throughput, while computational methods remain constrained by inconsistent evaluation and underperformance relative to simple baselines. Here we present DCAF, a unified framework for single-cell perturbation simulation that that jointly addresses data validity, evaluation validity and predictive modeling. Among its three components, DCAF-data addresses the single-measurement limitation by reconstructing pre- and post-perturbation status using entropy-regularized optimal transport, and is demonstrated on both cell line and multi-cell type datasets. DCAF-criterion evaluates log fold changes in non-silenced genes to improve sensitivity to model error and robustness to zero inflation noise, validated on synthetic datasets. DCAF-model combines JEPA with explicit modeling for regulatory-dynamics modeling for interpretable prediction. Across benchmarks, DCAF outperforms state-of-the-art deep-learning methods, as well as mean and linear baselines in cross-gene, cross-cell-type and cross-region generalization. In adult Mouse brain, DCAF recapitulates known cell-type-specific regulatory heterogeneity of Dgcr8 knockdown at both cell type and gene levels. DCAF thus provides a rigorous and biologically grounded foundation for reliable perturbation simulation across development, disease and therapeutic discovery.
affiliations: BGI Research, Wuhan (corresponding author)

papers.title: gene2fish: a multi-gene spatial expression browser for in situ hybridization data across zebrafish development
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) atlases of zebrafish development have catalogued marker genes for hundreds of cell types, but transcriptomic data alone cannot reveal their expression patterns in the embryo. The systematically annotated Thisse high-throughput whole-mount in situ hybridization (ISH) collection at ZFIN provides spatial expression data across twelve developmental stages, yet the ZFIN web interface is organized around individual genes, making side-by-side cross-gene comparison laborious. We present gene2fish, a web application that displays ISH images from the Thisse dataset, linked directly to their ZFIN records, in a gene-by-developmental-stage grid. With gene2fish, researchers can quickly explore and validate the spatial expression of marker gene lists, and find the genes annotated to specific anatomical structures across developmental time. The application is part of Zebrahub and is freely available at https://zebrahub.sf.czbiohub.org/gene2fish.
affiliations: Chan Zuckerberg Biohub San Francisco (corresponding author)

papers.title: Recombinant SIRT1 expression and SIRT1-METTL3 interaction analysis with computational identification of phytochemical SIRT1 activators and inhibitors
papers.abstract: Sirtuin 1 (SIRT1), a NAD{+/-}dependent histone deacetylase, regulates diverse biological processes including aging, stress response, and cancer progression. Owing to its dual roles in tumor suppression and promotion, selective modulators of SIRT1 have attracted considerable therapeutic interest. This study explored the interaction of SIRT1 with METTL3 and screened phytochemicals from Indian medicinal plants for potential SIRT1 activation or inhibition. Human SIRT1 (residues 183-665) was cloned, expressed in E. coli, purified, and validated by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) to confirm binding with METTL3. Computational approaches, including molecular docking, ADMET profiling, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, MM-PBSA free energy estimation, and frontier molecular orbital (FMO) analysis, were employed to characterize ligand interactions. Docking revealed Catechin, Epicatechin, Kaempferol, and Bisdemethoxycurcumin as potent inhibitors, showing stronger binding than the reference inhibitor Selisistat by stabilizing the catalytic pocket via key hydrogen bonds and {pi}-{pi} stacking interactions. Among activators, Ginsenosides and Carnosol demonstrated higher affinities than resveratrol, binding the allosteric site through hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions. MD simulations highlighted Catechin and Ginsenosides as the most stable modulators, supported by reduced RMSD, compact Rg values, and favorable hydrogen bond occupancy. MM-PBSA confirmed their strong binding free energies, while ADMET analysis predicted favorable pharmacokinetic properties and low toxicity, particularly for Catechin and Ginsenosides. Overall, this study integrates expression and purification of the protein and computational modeling to identify phytochemicals as potential SIRT1 modulators and provides novel insights into the SIRT1-METTL3 regulatory axis. These findings highlight Catechin and Ginsenosides as promising scaffolds for therapeutic strategies targeting cancer and metabolic disorders.
affiliations: Center for Advanced Interdisciplinary Science and Biomedicine of IHM, Division of Life Sciences and Medicine, University of Science and Technology of China, Hef (corresponding author)

papers.title: Europe and the rest of the world must come up with an answer to US science strategy
Bundle water safeguards into critical-mineral licences
Nobel-prizewinning breakthroughs can emerge from neglected organisms
Conservation planning should follow animal clocks
Nepal’s disaster is an urgent wake-up call
Will this sleep-disorder drug be the next big blockbuster?
Direct observation of the Lindhard continuum using resonant inelastic X-ray scattering
papers.abstract: In metals, the continuum of electron-hole excitations is described by the Lindhard function. Here, the authors directly observe the corresponding Lindhard continuum in the weakly correlated metal MgB2 using ultra-soft resonant inelastic X-ray scattering.

papers.title: Three-photon population imaging of subcortical brain regions
A prefrontal–bed nucleus pathway controls aversive memory specificity independently of glucocorticoids
papers.abstract: Adaptive memory requires balancing generalization to avoid similar threats with discrimination to recognize safety. The prevailing view is that stress-induced increases in glucocorticoids underlie the enhancement of memory consolidation, strengthening memories and promoting their generalization—referred to here as the standard model. However, circuits that drive memory consolidation often also regulate glucocorticoid release, confounding whether their effects on memory are circuit-driven or hormonally mediated. Here we identify a prefrontal pathway that controls memory specificity independently of glucocorticoids. Using optogenetic manipulations in male rats, we found that post-training inhibition of the rostral prelimbic cortex (rPL) to anteroventral bed nuclei of the stria terminalis (avBST) pathway promoted contextual generalization in an inhibitory avoidance discrimination task without affecting memory strength. Although this manipulation further elevated corticosterone, it produced generalization even in adrenalectomized rats, demonstrating glucocorticoid independence. Conversely, post-training pathway excitation enhanced contextual discrimination. Recordings of calcium signals revealed context-specific engagement of both avBST and avBST-projecting rPL neurons during memory retrieval, with greater responses in the neutral than the aversive context. These findings reveal glucocorticoid-independent circuit control of memory specificity, setting boundary conditions on the standard model and demonstrating mechanistic heterogeneity that may inform stress-related disorders where memory generalization is a core feature.

papers.title: Strong field spectroscopy of many-body interactions in solids
papers.abstract: High-order harmonic generation (HHG) in solids offers a promising route to compact ultrafast sources of quantum light, but its efficiency and coherence are limited by ultrafast dephasing of laser-driven electron–hole polarization. Although widely described by a phenomenological coherence time, the microscopic origin of this dephasing has remained unresolved. Here, we combine wavelength-dependent HHG measurements in monolayer and bulk semiconductors with ab initio many-body calculations of electron–phonon scattering and strong-field simulations. We show that the measured wavelength scaling of the HHG yield is quantitatively reproduced only when semiconductor Bloch equations incorporate momentum-dependent dephasing derived from first principles scattering rates. The calculations reveal that strong-field-driven carriers rapidly enter regions of the Brillouin zone with enhanced electron–phonon scattering, giving rise to effective few-femtosecond dephasing. Our results establish a microscopic foundation for dephasing in solid-state HHG and provide a framework for engineering coherence in strongly driven solids for quantum photonic applications.

papers.title: Balancing the Performance Trade-off of Polymer Blends with Heterogeneously Dispersed Nanodomains via Reactive Processing
papers.abstract: Polymer blends are ubiquitous though there are persistent material-property trade-offs, due to structural design. Here the authors design multicomponent polymers optimizing the material properties.

papers.title: Nutrient stress-driven ACSS1 controls metabolic flexibility and bone formation
Production of abundant defective viral genomes by an insect-specific alphavirus revealed by nanopore sequencing
Terahertz emission by X-ray difference-frequency generation
papers.abstract: Nonlinear interactions between X-rays and matter represent a new frontier in ultrafast science. However, X-ray difference-frequency generation (DFG)—a fundamental second-order nonlinear optical process—has not been experimentally observed until now. Here, we report the first observation of terahertz emission induced by hard X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) pulses in solids, providing evidence for X-ray DFG. Using 10-fs, 10-keV XFEL pulses incident on ZnTe, we detected terahertz emission arising from wave mixing between different spectral components within the XFEL bandwidth. The emitted terahertz waves originate from second-order nonlinear polarization evolving on a femtosecond timescale. The polarization and angular dependences of the terahertz emission confirm that X-ray DFG is mediated not only by DFG without spatial inversion symmetry but also by DFG with spatial inversion symmetry. Quantitative analysis yields a DFG susceptibility ratio of the former to the latter of 58±4%, and the generation efficiency for 10 keV excitation is approximately 1% of that for near-infrared 1.55 eV excitation in the 100-μm-thick ZnTe crystal, while the intrinsic response normalized by interaction length is comparable. These results establish XFEL-induced terahertz emission as a general platform for probing second-order X-ray nonlinearities and ultrafast polarization dynamics in solids.

papers.title: Comprehensive spectroscopic analysis of energy inversion of the lowest singlet and triplet excited states in the heptazine HzTFEX2
papers.abstract: Detailed photophysical measurements of the non-symmetric heptazine, HzTFEX 2 , previously reported as having inverted S 1 -T 1 levels, show complex behaviour, highly dependent on environment, concentration and aggregation. Here we show that, single crystals of HzTFEX 2 show anti-Kasha S 0 ←S 2 and excimer emission. Solution state absorption shows a hypsochromic shift of the π-π* S 0 →S 1 , linearly dependent on solvent polarizability. In most environments, emission is dominated by excimer species, only in toluene and frozen 2-MeTHF do monomeric properties dominate. In frozen solutions, aggregation phenomena are solvent dependent. Given such complexity, time-dependent emission spectra are crowded, making it difficult to resolve monomeric phosphorescence. However, by exciting S 0 →S 2 at 77 K, we observe a consistent phosphorescence signal at 425 nm, 110 ± 20 meV above the S 0 ←S 1 emission, whereas exciting S 0 →S 1 does not give phosphorescence or delayed fluorescence (DF). We conclude that coupling between S 2 and S 1 is very weak, S 2 -T N intersystem crossing is effective, whereas S 1 ↔T 1 intersystem crossing is thermally activated, fulfilling the conditions required for the observation of inverted phosphorescence. At room temperature, no long-lived DF is observed because exothermic T 1 →S 1 ISC becomes allowed, such that in an OLED, high efficiency can be achieved.

papers.title: The Emirati pangenome featuring a diploid chromosome-level reference
G-quadruplex structures affect the immune response to bacterial infection in mouse macrophages
papers.abstract: Macrophages orchestrate immunity via transcriptional reprogramming, largely controlled by the master regulator NF-κB. However, mechanisms of promoter selection remain enigmatic. Here, we reveal that DNA secondary structures called G-quadruplexes (G4s) modulate the macrophage transcriptome during inflammation. By investigating the G4 ligand pyridostatin (PDS) in lipopolysaccharide-stimulated macrophages, we establish that G4 stabilization significantly decreases the inflammatory response without affecting mitochondrial metabolism or pathogen clearance. Instead, NF-κB-dependent transcription of activation markers and proinflammatory cytokines is selectively repressed. Using chromatin accessibility profiling, NF-κB ChIP, and in silico predictions, we demonstrate that G4 stabilization sterically hinders NF-κB promoter occupancy. Furthermore, PDS stabilizes transient, transcription-induced G4s, prematurely shutting down transcription and reverting local chromatin to a dormant state. Thus, G4 formation represents a potential strategy to modulate dysregulated macrophage activation.

papers.title: Anterior cingulate input tunes striatal dynamics for context-dependent social preference in a mouse model of autism
papers.abstract: The mechanisms underlying social behavioural deficits in mouse models of autism are not fully understood. Here the authors link neural embedding geometry to context-dependent social deficits in the Shank3 knockout mouse.

papers.title: Terahertz field-induced giant symmetry modulations in a van der Waals antiferromagnet
papers.abstract: Strong-field terahertz (THz) excitations enable dynamic control over electronic, lattice and symmetry degrees of freedom in quantum materials. Here, we uncover pronounced terahertz-induced symmetry modulations and coherent phonon dynamics in the van der Waals antiferromagnet MnPS 3 , in which inversion symmetry is broken by its antiferromagnetic spin configuration. Our time-resolved second harmonic generation measurements reveal long-lived giant oscillations in the antiferromagnetic phase, with amplitudes comparable to the equilibrium signal, driven by phonons involving percent-level atomic displacements relative to the equilibrium bond lengths. The temporal evolution of the rotational anisotropy patterns indicates a dynamic breaking of mirror symmetry, modulated by two vibrational modes at 1.7 THz and 4.5 THz, with the former corresponding to a hidden mode not observed in equilibrium spectroscopy. These effects arise in part from a field-induced charge rearrangement mechanism that lowers the local crystal symmetry and couples to the phonon modes. We uncover a long-lived field-driven response with a complex THz polarization dependence, consistent with a metastable state of reduced symmetry. Through comparison with simulations, we interpret this response in terms of a potential antiferromagnetic-to-ferrimagnetic transition. Our results establish an effective field-tunable pathway for driving excitations otherwise weak in equilibrium.

papers.title: Fatty acids in the tumor microenvironment reprogram neutrophils to induce adenosine-mediated immunosuppression in mice
papers.abstract: Lipid accumulation in solid tumors supports tumor progression by promoting immune evasion. Yet the molecular basis of this lipid-mediated immunosuppression remains unclear. Here, using murine models of advanced colorectal cancer, the authors uncover a metabolic-immune axis whereby tumor-derived fatty acids activate neutrophil PPARα, resulting in adenosine generation and T cell suppression. Importantly, treatment with a dual adenosine receptor antagonist restores T cell-mediated antitumor immunity and synergizes with anti-PD-1 therapy to enhance animal survival.

papers.title: Divergent anaerobic fates of biodegradable plastics in landfill leachate
papers.abstract: How different biodegradable plastics break down within landfills, particularly landfill leachate, remain unclear. Here, they evaluated the anaerobic biodegradability of three BPs, polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB), poly(lactic acid) (PLA), and poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), using a combination of genome-resolved multi-omics.

papers.title: Oncogenic signalling and host immunocompetency govern senescent cell clearance and systemic inflammation in a mouse model of oncogene-induced senescence
papers.abstract: Senescence is a stress-induced program defined by permanent cell-cycle arrest and a pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Defective clearance of senescent cells promotes inflammation, tissue dysfunction, and ageing, yet determinants of their elimination remain poorly understood. Here, we model oncogene-induced senescence in the hematopoietic system by transplanting Braf V600E - or Braf ΔN -expressing hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells into recipients with distinct immune backgrounds. Braf V600E induces a stronger senescence program and more aggressive disease than Braf ΔN . Survival depends on oncogene-expressing cell burden and host immunity: immunocompetent, lower-burden mice clear oncogene-expressing cells and survive long-term, whereas higher-burden mice show checkpoint upregulation, T-cell exhaustion, and early death. NSG, Rag1KO, and lymphocyte-depleted hosts fail to clear these cells, developing sustained inflammation and bone marrow failure. Rapamycin administration attenuates senescence-associated features and improves survival. These findings identify oncogenic intensity and adaptive immune competence as coupled determinants of senescent-cell fate, with implications for chronic inflammation and senescence-targeted therapies.

papers.title: Large-scale proteomic characterization reveals clinically relevant subtypes of early-stage papillary thyroid cancer for prognostic prediction
Peripheral glia drive the initiation of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
papers.abstract: Although tumor innervation is known to promote cancer progression, underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood and have mostly been linked to axonal signaling. Here, we identify peripheral glia as critical drivers of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), the second most common skin cancer in humans. Tumor-associated glial cells (TAGs) resemble embryonic Schwann cell lineage stages, are abundant in the stroma of premalignant lesions and established murine and human cSCC, and are essential for tumor formation. TAG activation in premalignant lesions is triggered by UV-induced anti-inflammatory macrophages, which in turn are polarized by TAGs into pro-tumorigenic FcεRIα⁺ macrophages, key components of the cSCC microenvironment. Consequently, TAG depletion reduces FcεRIα⁺ macrophages, cancer-associated fibroblasts, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition in keratinocytes, thereby impairing cSCC initiation by disrupting intercellular communication required for tumor development. As most solid tumors are innervated and harbor peripheral glia, our findings reveal TAGs as regulators of tumor initiation with potential relevance beyond skin cancer.

papers.title: Human hemoglobin protects the parasite cytoskeleton during Plasmodium falciparum gametocyte development
papers.abstract: Wang et al. apply single particle cryo-EM to developing gametocytes of Plasmodium falciparum, and identify human hemoglobin as a prominent factor that binds to P. falciparum subpellicular microtubule (SPMT) network.

papers.title: Epithelial NF-κB shapes protective Treg cell responses to restrain intestinal inflammation
papers.abstract: Inflammation resolution depends on coordinated communication between tissue compartments, yet how the intestinal epithelium shapes its immune microenvironment remains poorly understood. Here, using colonic biopsies from patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) and mouse models enabling tissue-wide visualization of NF-κB activity, we combine single-cell RNA sequencing and secretome analysis to define epithelial communication during colitis. We show that, paradoxically, the NF-κB-driven pro-inflammatory secretome of intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) is essential for recovery and prevents unrestrained inflammation. Mechanistically, epithelial NF-κB promotes CCL22-dependent regulatory T cell (Treg cell) recruitment and promotes a tolerogenic, pro-repair cell state, accompanied by induction of the lipid-metabolism-associated GDPD3 and CCR4. In UC, epithelial NF-κB is not uniformly activated but instead induces a selective pro-inflammatory transcriptional program while repressing targets regulating T cell recruitment. Thus, we identify dynamic epithelial–immune communication and demonstrate a protective IEC NF-κB–Treg cell axis important for resolution of intestinal inflammation.

papers.title: Identification and genetic characterization of megabase-scale plasmids of Enterobacteriaceae
papers.abstract: Humans and animals are ubiquitously colonized by Enterobacteriaceae , including both commensals and clinically significant pathogens. Here, we report 21 complete Enterobacteriaceae megaplasmid genomes of up to 1.58 Mbp in length spanning two major clades that are highly divergent from previously described plasmids. Of these, three were reconstructed from isolates of Escherichia coli and Shigella flexneri ; others were potentially hosted by species of Citrobacter and Enterobacter . Related megabase-scale plasmids were detected in at least 400 infant and adult gut, and other microbiomes. Diverse Enterobacteriaceae hosts, conjugation machinery, and DNA modification patterns suggest that these elements are self-transmissible, with a broad host range. The plasmids encode multi-drug efflux systems and potential secreted effectors. Up to 208 tRNAs are encoded and include sequence variants that may counter tRNA-centric defense mechanisms. Overall, the vast plasmid coding capacity may broaden host range, increase competitiveness, control invasion by other elements, and counter programmed cell death.

papers.title: High-risk antimicrobial resistance genomic traits in multidrug-resistant Salmonella across China’s food chain: projections to 2050
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is rising globally, yet factors shaping its genomic evolution remain poorly understood. We investigated how socioeconomic, climate, and health factors are associated with AMR spread in multi-drug resistant (MDR) Salmonella enterica across China’s food chain, mapped hotspots and forecasted genomic trait prevalence to 2050. We analysed 2,536 MDR genomes from 15 provinces over 16 years, covering patients, food and non-food workers, meat, livestock, and environmental sources. A machine learning framework integrated genomic surveillance with risk assessment to identify high-risk AMR traits (clinically relevant, MDR, mobile). Regression models linked trait prevalence to socioeconomic, climate, health, and antimicrobial consumption data, informing projections to 2050. Eighty-four high-risk traits, including carbapenem, colistin, and β-lactam resistance, are projected to rise, with antibiotic use, population growth, healthcare spending, and urbanisation. Projections were trait-specific: bla CTX-M-64 and bla TEM-1 may increase up to 20%, while bla CTX-M-65 and bla CTX-M-14 remain below 5%. A mechanistic shift in fluoroquinolone resistance is projected: mutation-based resistance ( gyrA 87) declines while plasmid-mediated genes ( qnrB17 , qnrS1 ) rise. Food workers emerged as a potential reservoir, showing higher trait prevalence than food sources, uniquely carrying last-resort antibiotic-resistance genes ( bla TEM-30 , bla NDM-5 , bla CTX-M-64 ). Integrating genomic with socioeconomic surveillance could shift AMR interventions from reactive to preventive.

papers.title: Multiancestry conditional and joint analysis applied to GWAS summary statistics
papers.abstract: Conditional and joint (COJO) analysis of genome-wide association study (GWAS) data is a standard post-GWAS analysis for identifying statistically independent associations. Although GWAS meta-analyses are increasingly conducted across multiple ancestry groups, the optimal strategy for multiancestry COJO analysis remains unclear. Here we introduce Manc-COJO, a method for multiancestry COJO analysis. Simulations and real-data analyses show that Manc-COJO improves detection of independent association signals while reducing false positives compared with single-ancestry COJO implemented in genome-wide complex trait analysis (GCTA) and its ad-hoc multiancestry adaptations. We also introduce Manc-COJO:FIX, a follow-up algorithm to identify ancestry-specific independent associations. The C++ implementation of Manc-COJO is over 120-fold faster than GCTA-COJO and supports linkage disequilibrium references derived from either individual-level genotype data or pre-computed matrices, facilitating analyses when data sharing is limited.

papers.title: The landscape of gene loss and missense variation across the mammalian tree informs on gene essentiality
papers.abstract: Patterns of gene and sequence preservation across species provide insight into gene essentiality under natural selection. Here we developed two interspecies constraint metrics across 462 mammalian species: Gene Identity Score of Mammalian Orthologs (GISMO), which quantifies gene loss weighted by evolutionary distance to humans, and GISMO-mis, which measures missense constraint using the ratio of missense to synonymous variation across mammals. Both metrics are strongly correlated with human loss of function, missense and dosage constraint derived from large-scale sequencing studies, yet are largely independent of coding sequence length. GISMO and GISMO-mis identify essential genes missed by existing human-only metrics, particularly short genes. Genes in the most constrained deciles are enriched for rare variant associations in disorders linked to reduced fecundity, including schizophrenia, autism and neurodevelopmental disorders, and show strong enrichment for common variant heritability. These deciles also exhibit reduced copy number variation, consistent with dosage sensitivity. In addition, GISMO improves prioritization of recessive disease genes and captures signatures of homozygous selection across the mammalian tree. Taken together, GISMO and GISMO-mis leverage deep mammalian evolution to provide complementary, length-robust measures of gene essentiality that strengthen disease–gene prioritization and illuminate the selective forces shaping human biology.

papers.title: Mechanism of M18BP1-mediated activation of condensin II for mitotic DNA compaction
papers.abstract: Here, the authors show that phosphorylated M18BP1 activates condensin II by relieving an autoinhibitory interface, enabling stable DNA binding and compaction. Additionally, the M18BP1–condensin II complex forms clusters that might mechanically reinforce mitotic chromosomes.

papers.title: Phosphorylated M18BP1 activates autoinhibited condensin II to drive mitotic DNA compaction
papers.abstract: By integrating cryo-electron microscopy with single molecule studies, we show that phosphorylated MIS18-binding protein 1 (M18BP1P) relieves condensin II from an autoinhibitory conformation, enabling stable DNA binding and ATP hydrolysis-dependent DNA compaction. In addition, M18BP1–condensin II complex multimers substantially contribute to DNA compaction and might provide mechanical reinforcement of mitotic chromosomes.

papers.title: Electrolytes that mind bridging the gap
papers.abstract: Silicon anodes enable high-energy-density Li-ion batteries but face reversibility challenges when operating under extreme temperature and charge-rate conditions. Now, a liquid electrolyte design results in interface protection and reduced electrode expansion during such operation, while also having lithium plating tolerance.

papers.title: Small variant calling in the era of long-read sequencing
papers.abstract: Long-read sequencing is expanding the scope of small-variant detection, enabling analysis of genomic regions that were previously difficult to interrogate. In this Review, the authors examine approaches for long-read small-variant calling across sequencing platforms and applications, highlighting advances in deep learning, assembly-based and pangenome-based methods, benchmarking strategies and future challenges.
